title: Anomaly Detection
summary: Finding rare, abnormal points without relying on labeled examples of them — the statistical, tree-based, and neural approaches interviewers probe.

slides.markdown:
**Anomaly detection** finds the rare points that don't look like the rest — a fraudulent transaction, a failing sensor, an intruder in network traffic — usually **without** a labeled set of past anomalies to train on.

That missing-labels constraint is what makes it a distinct problem from ordinary classification: you're modeling what "normal" looks like, then flagging anything that doesn't fit.

slides.subTitle: Anomalies as low probability
slides.markdown:
The core idea: model the **probability distribution** of normal data, then flag any point that falls in a **low-probability region** as anomalous.

This reframes an otherwise vague question — "is this weird?" — into something measurable: rare means unlikely under the distribution the rest of your data follows. Every technique in this topic is a different way of estimating that distribution, or approximating "how unlikely is this point" without fully modeling it.

slides.subTitle: z-score and IQR
slides.markdown:
For a single numeric feature, two cheap, interpretable flags work surprisingly well:

- **z-score** — how many standard deviations a point sits from the mean; flag anything beyond roughly ±3.
- **IQR (interquartile range)** — flag points below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR, which is more robust to a distribution that isn't bell-shaped.

Both are per-feature and assume the data is roughly unimodal — they miss anomalies that only show up in the *combination* of several features.

slides.subTitle: Isolating by random partitioning
slides.markdown:
An **isolation forest** builds many random trees that split the data on random features at random thresholds. Anomalies get isolated into their own leaf in **very few splits**, because they sit far from the bulk of the data — normal points take many more splits to separate out.

A point's average path length across the whole forest becomes its anomaly score: short average path → anomaly; long average path → normal. It scales well and needs no assumption about the data's distribution shape, which is why it's a common production default.

slides.subTitle: Anomalies as reconstruction error
slides.markdown:
An **autoencoder** (see [Autoencoders & Generative Basics](autoencoders-generative-basics)) learns to compress and reconstruct *normal* data well, since that's what it was trained on. Feed it an anomaly and the reconstruction tends to be noticeably worse, because the network never learned to represent that pattern efficiently.

That gap — the **reconstruction error** — becomes the anomaly score. This approach shines on high-dimensional, complex data like images or sensor time-series, where simple statistical methods can't capture the structure at all.

slides.subTitle: When labels are scarce
slides.markdown:
| | Supervised fraud classification | Unsupervised anomaly detection |
|---|---|---|
| Needs labeled anomalies | Yes, and enough of them | No |
| Catches novel anomaly types | Only ones resembling training examples | Yes — flags anything unlike normal |
| Typical accuracy on known patterns | Higher | Lower |
| Best when | Plenty of confirmed fraud cases exist | Fraud is rare, new, or evolving fast |

**How to decide:** with a healthy set of confirmed labels, supervised classification usually wins on precision; with few or no labels — or fraud patterns that keep changing — unsupervised anomaly detection is the only option that generalizes to *new* kinds of anomalies.

slides.subTitle: Accuracy on the rare class
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My anomaly detector is 99.5% accurate, so it's working well."

**Why it's wrong:** if anomalies are 0.5% of the data, a detector that flags **nothing at all** already hits 99.5% accuracy — while catching zero real anomalies. Accuracy on a rare class is nearly meaningless.

**Correct model:** evaluate with **precision and recall** on the anomaly class specifically (and precision-recall curves over a threshold sweep), so you can see the actual trade-off between catching anomalies and drowning analysts in false alarms.

slides.sectionTitle: Setting the threshold: a business decision, not a statistics one
slides.markdown:
Every anomaly score needs a cutoff above which something gets flagged, and that cutoff is really a trade-off between two costs: a false positive (an analyst wastes time investigating a normal transaction) versus a false negative (real fraud goes uncaught). Those costs are rarely symmetric — missing a $50,000 fraud is usually far worse than 20 analysts spending 10 minutes each clearing false alarms.

In practice, the threshold gets tuned against the actual downstream cost, often by walking the precision-recall curve and picking the point where the combined cost (false-positive investigation time x false-positive rate, plus false-negative loss x false-negative rate) is lowest — not by picking a statistically "natural" cutoff like a z-score of 3.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: anomalies contaminating the "normal" training data
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I trained my isolation forest / autoencoder on all historical data, so it correctly models normal behavior."

**Why it's wrong:** if the historical training data already contains some undetected anomalies (which it usually does — that's often exactly why you're building the detector), the model partially learns to treat those anomalies as normal, raising the bar for what counts as unusual and quietly reducing recall on the anomaly type that's already sneaking through.

**Correct model:** where possible, train on a period or subset believed to be clean, and periodically re-audit training data for contamination — an anomaly detector is only as good as its definition of normal, and that definition degrades silently if the training set isn't actually anomaly-free.
